name: Tsomgo Lake
tagline: A glacial lake at 3,750 m on the road to the Nathu La
meta_description: Tsomgo (Changu) Lake guide: permits, Nathu La and Baba Mandir, costs from Gangtok, altitude, best months and what to expect on the day trip.
summary: Tsomgo, also called Changu, is a glacial lake at about 3,750 m, 40 km east of Gangtok on the road to the Nathu La. It is visited as a permit day trip with a registered Gangtok agency. Indians can add the Nathu La border pass and Baba Mandir. Go early; the lake freezes in mid-winter.
intro: The road from Gangtok to Tsomgo climbs about 2,000 m in 40 km, past army camps, waterfalls and the Kyongnosla alpine sanctuary, to a lake held in a bowl of steep slopes. Tsomgo is roughly oval, about a kilometre long, and is fed by snowmelt from the surrounding ridges. In winter it freezes over; in May and June the slopes around it bloom with rhododendrons and primulas.

For the Bhutia communities of East Sikkim the lake is sacred, and lamas once read the colour of its water to foretell the future. Today its shore is lined with tea stalls, yak handlers and stalls renting boots and coats, and the morning hours are the quietest. A small shrine stands near the water.

Tsomgo lies inside a protected area near the border with Tibet, so every visitor needs a permit issued in advance through a registered travel agency in Gangtok, and private self-driven cars from outside Sikkim are not usually allowed. Indian nationals can continue on permitted days to the Nathu La at 4,310 m and the Baba Harbhajan Singh shrine. Check current status before you travel.
facts: Frozen winter lake, yaks, Nathu La, Baba Mandir

highlights.title: The lake in early light
highlights.text: Arrive by 9 am, before the vehicles stack up, and walk the path along the eastern shore. On still mornings the water mirrors the ridges; in January and February the surface is frozen white and snow lines the road.

highlights.title: The Nathu La border pass
highlights.text: Indian nationals with the right permit can drive on to the Nathu La at 4,310 m, the pass on the old trade route to Lhasa and a border post between India and China. Visits have usually run Wednesday to Sunday; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Baba Harbhajan Singh Mandir
highlights.text: A shrine to an Indian Army soldier who died in the area in 1968, now venerated by soldiers and visitors who leave water bottles and offerings. It sits on the Nathu La road and is part of most extended Tsomgo trips.

highlights.title: Spring flowers at Kyongnosla
highlights.text: Below the lake, the Kyongnosla alpine sanctuary protects rhododendron, primula and other high-altitude plants. From April to June the roadside is in flower, and the air smells of juniper.

highlights.title: Yaks on the shore
highlights.text: Decorated yaks wait by the lake for short rides. If you ride, agree the price first and keep it short; at this altitude even a slow walk takes effort.

field_notes.fact: The name Tsomgo is usually translated from Bhutia as source of the lake. The lake is fed by melting snow from the surrounding mountains and freezes over in winter.
On Guru Purnima, jhakris, the traditional faith healers of Sikkim, gather at Tsomgo, which is believed to have healing properties.
Border trade over the Nathu La was halted in 1962 and reopened in 2006, for the first time in 44 years, with a trade mart at Sherathang below the pass.

how_to_reach.text: Tsomgo is about 40 km from Gangtok on the Jawaharlal Nehru Road towards the Nathu La, 1.5–2 hours each way. Only Sikkim-registered tourist vehicles with permits go through the check post, so book through a registered agency. Snow and landslides close the road some days; check current status before you travel.

Many Gangtok agencies sell seats in shared jeeps leaving around 7–8 am and returning by early afternoon. It is the cheapest way to go if you are travelling alone or as a couple. Give your ID and photos to the agency the day before.
The nearest commercial airport is Bagdogra, about 165 km away. You must first reach Gangtok, spend the night, and arrange your permit there; same-day trips from Siliguri are not possible.

where_to_stay: There is no tourist accommodation at Tsomgo and overnight stays are not permitted in this protected area. Visit as a day trip from Gangtok and choose your stay there: guesthouses near Tibet Road for saver travellers, Hotel Tibet or Netuk House for comfort, and the Elgin Nor-Khill or Mayfair for signature trips. Leave Gangtok early to reach the lake before the crowds.
tips: Give your agency a copy of photo ID and two passport photos the day before; permits are issued for named passengers and a specific vehicle.
Start by 7 am; permit checks and traffic slow the road after 9 am in season.
Carry warm layers, sunglasses and sunscreen even in summer; wind at 3,750 m is cold.
Do not take children under about five or anyone with heart or lung trouble to Nathu La without talking to a doctor.
Do not throw anything into the lake, and carry your plastic back to Gangtok.

experiences.title: A slow walk around Tsomgo's shore
experiences.cost: Permit and vehicle through Gangtok agency
experiences.summary: Walk the shore path at Tsomgo while the light is low and the stalls are still opening. In winter you see a frozen lake and snowfields; in late spring, rhododendron and primula on the slopes. Keep the pace slow and your hands warm.
body: Most vehicles stop at the north end of the lake, where tea stalls and yak handlers gather. A path runs along part of the shore, and it is worth walking a few hundred metres away from the stalls to see the lake as the locals describe it: a quiet, sacred water in a ring of steep, scrub-covered slopes.

The lake changes completely with the seasons. From about January to March the surface is usually frozen and the slopes white. In April and May the ice breaks and flowers start; in October and November the water is clear and the sky deep blue. The monsoon months bring cloud and rain, and the road is often blocked.

Altitude is the main thing to respect. At about 3,750 m, a short climb leaves you breathless, especially if you arrived in Gangtok the day before. Walk slowly, drink water and do not run in the snow. If you feel a strong headache, nausea or dizziness, go back down; symptoms usually ease quickly as you descend.

faqs.a: The lake usually freezes from about late December to March, depending on the winter. Heavy snow in this period can also close the road for days. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight at Tsomgo Lake?
faqs.a: No, overnight stays are not permitted. Tsomgo is visited as a day trip from Gangtok with a permit, and vehicles must return the same afternoon.

faqs.q: Is Tsomgo Lake safe for seniors?
faqs.a: Most healthy seniors manage a short visit, as you drive to the shore. The altitude of about 3,750 m can still cause breathlessness or headache. Walk slowly and talk to your doctor before going if you have heart or lung conditions.

experiences.title: Nathu La, the pass on the Lhasa road
experiences.cost: Vehicle ₹6,000–9,000 incl. Tsomgo; permit via agency
experiences.summary: Continue past Tsomgo to the Nathu La at 4,310 m, the pass on the old Kalimpong–Lhasa trade route and today a border post between India and China. It is open only to Indian nationals with a permit, on set days, and the visit is short and cold.
body: From Tsomgo the road climbs another 17 km or so through bare, rocky country to the pass. On the Indian side there is a memorial, a viewing area and, in good weather, a view down into the Chumbi valley of Tibet. Army staff manage the area and set the rules, which can include limits on photography and on time at the top.

Nathu La was one of the main passes between Sikkim and Tibet, used by traders carrying wool and salt down and cloth and goods up. Border trade stopped in 1962 and reopened in 2006, through a trade mart at Sherathang below the pass, and it runs in the summer season when permitted. The pass also forms part of one route for Kailash Mansarovar pilgrims when that route is open.

Permits are issued only to Indian nationals and only through registered agencies in Gangtok, usually for specific days of the week, often Wednesday to Sunday. Snow, weather and security decisions can cancel visits at short notice. At 4,310 m, the risk of altitude sickness is real: no running, plenty of water, and talk to your doctor first if you have health conditions. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: No. Nathu La has been open only to Indian nationals, with a Protected Area Permit arranged through a registered Gangtok agency. Foreigners can usually visit Tsomgo Lake instead. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: On which days is Nathu La open for tourists?
faqs.a: Tourist visits have usually been allowed Wednesday to Sunday, with Monday and Tuesday closed, but weather and security can change this at short notice. Ask your agency and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long can I stay at Nathu La?
faqs.a: Visits are short, typically 30–60 minutes at the top, set by the army and your permit. The altitude of 4,310 m also makes a longer stay unwise for most people.

experiences.title: Baba Harbhajan Singh Mandir
experiences.cost: Included in vehicle cost; permit via agency
experiences.summary: Stop at the shrine honouring Harbhajan Singh, an Indian Army soldier who died in this area in 1968. Soldiers posted on this frontier treat him as a guardian spirit, and visitors leave water bottles and offerings to take home blessed.
body: The shrine lies on the road between Tsomgo and the Nathu La, at around 4,000 m, and is managed by the Indian Army. A newer memorial building with a small museum stands by the road, and the original bunker site is further up. Inside, his uniform, boots and bed are kept as if he were still on duty, and the regiment honours him in its own traditions.

Visitors come from across India, and many leave bottles of water at the shrine to be collected later and taken home as blessed water. There is often a small canteen run by the army, with tea and snacks. It is a place of respect for soldiers and their families, so keep voices low and follow any instructions from staff.

Most Tsomgo trips include the shrine, either on its own or with the Nathu La. The permit covers it, but access depends on the day's road and security situation. Dress warmly; the wind here is strong in all seasons.

faqs.q: Is Baba Mandir included in the Tsomgo permit?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Most Gangtok agencies offer Tsomgo plus Baba Mandir as a standard trip, with Nathu La as an extra for Indian nationals. Confirm what your permit covers when you book.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Baba Harbhajan Singh Mandir?
faqs.a: Access for foreigners depends on the permit rules in force, as the shrine lies beyond Tsomgo in the Nathu La area. Ask your agency and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long does the Tsomgo and Baba Mandir trip take?
faqs.a: Allow 6–8 hours from Gangtok, leaving around 7 am and returning by early afternoon. Adding Nathu La takes a little longer.

faqs.q: How do I get a permit for Tsomgo Lake?
faqs.a: Book through a registered travel agency or your Gangtok hotel at least a day ahead with a photo ID and two passport photos. The agency applies for the Protected Area Permit and provides the vehicle. Foreigners need a minimum group size, usually two. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Tsomgo Lake from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 40 km, 1.5–2 hours each way on a winding mountain road. Most trips leave at 7–8 am and return by early or mid-afternoon.

faqs.q: What is the cost of a Tsomgo Lake trip?
faqs.a: A seat in a shared jeep costs about ₹800–1,500 per person. A private vehicle for Tsomgo and Baba Mandir is about ₹3,500–5,500, and with Nathu La ₹6,000–9,000. Rates rise in peak season.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Tsomgo Lake?
faqs.a: For a frozen lake and snow, late December to March; for flowers and clear water, April to May; for the clearest skies, October and November. Avoid July and August, when landslides and fog often stop trips.

faqs.q: Is Tsomgo Lake open in winter?
faqs.a: Usually, but heavy snowfall closes the road for a day or several days at a time, especially in January and February. Permits are issued daily depending on conditions; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness at Tsomgo Lake?
faqs.a: Some people feel headache or breathlessness at 3,750 m, especially after flying in. Spend at least one night in Gangtok first, move slowly and drink water. Talk to your doctor before going if you have heart or lung conditions, are pregnant or travelling with infants.

faqs.q: Can I drive my own car to Tsomgo Lake?
faqs.a: Generally no. Only Sikkim-registered tourist vehicles with permits are allowed beyond the check post. Plan to hire a local vehicle and driver through an agency.

faqs.q: Is there a mobile network at Tsomgo Lake?
faqs.a: Coverage is limited and varies by provider; some networks work near the lake and around the army areas, others do not. Do not rely on mobile data for payments; carry cash.

faqs.q: What should I wear to Tsomgo Lake?
faqs.a: Warm layers, a windproof jacket, gloves and a cap in any season, plus sunglasses and sunscreen. Waterproof shoes help in snow; boots and coats can be rented at the lake and on the way.
